newsitem.title: USA: N. Korea to respond next week on peace proposal.
newsitem.headline: N. Korea to respond next week on peace proposal.

text.p: North Korea has promised to give its response next week to a U.S.-South Korea proposal for peace talks, the State Department said on Thursday.
Spokesman Nicholas Burns said delegations from all three countries would meet in New York on April 16 and the United States hoped the North Korean response would be positive.
He also told reporters the United States expected to announce new food aid for North Korea next week.

"As for food aid, we are now working with several agencies of our government to develop our response to the WFP (World Food Program) food appeal. I would expect by next week we would have an answer," Burns said.

The United States and South Korea proposed four-party talks on April 19, 1996 as a way to defuse tensions on the Korean peninsula and get to a peace treaty that would finally close the books on the 1950-53 war that divided the peninsula. China would also take part in the negotiations.
"This is not a briefing. This is a meeting. They have requested the meeting," Burns told reporters.
"We hope it's going to be positive although they have not indicated to us as far as I know what their essential response will be," he said.
After the meeting of U.S., North Korean and South Korean delegations, the United States and North Korea will hold bilateral talks.

Those will focus on American servicemen missing in action from the Korean War, U.S. concerns about North Korean missile sales and establishment of liaison offices in each other's capitals, Burns said.

Pyongyang's decision to give a formal response to the peace talks proposal came at a time of heightened international concern about food shortages in the isolated, Stalinist-ruled country and of greater willingness by the United States and other countries to give humanitarian aid.

The World Food Programme has called for $95.5 million for 200,000 tons of food and U.S. officials -- noting a positive U.S. response to all previous appeals -- have virtually assured that more U.S. aid will be forthcoming.
Washington has provided $18.4 million since late 1995, including a $10 million donation now being shipped to Pyongyang.

The Washington Post reported on Thursday that the Pentagon's intelligence agency has estimated that as many as 100,000 North Koreans may die from starvation and related diseases in the next four months.
A State Department official said "it's clear there is a serious urgent problem" in North Korea but was unaware of the Defence Intelligence Agency estimates.
